newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Dutch bourses join forces in run-up to EMU.
newsitem.headline: Dutch bourses join forces in run-up to EMU.

text.p: Amsterdam's stock exchange, the world's oldest bourse, on Friday announced plans to join forces with a younger partner, the European Options Exchange (EOE), to fight off increasingly fierce foreign competition in the run-up to European Economic and Monetary Union.

"The intended merger is aimed at giving the Amsterdam securities and derivatives market a more solid foundation in the light of growing international competition," the two bourses said in a joint statement.
Preliminary merger plans were given the go-ahead by the exchanges' respective executive councils on Thursday night, paving the way for a full-blown merger by the end of the year.
"(The councils) have agreed that we need to come to a merger on the basis of equal input," Amsterdam bourse spokesman Herman de Ranitz said.
"The final decision is subject to members' approval but it would be very odd if (the merger) did not go ahead," he said.
EOE spokesman Lex van Drooge agreed, saying there were sufficient grounds for assuming members would approve the plans.
For the stock exchange, the planned merger represents the latest in a string of initiatives to ensure it retains a competitive edge as the European market opens up.

Ranked fifth among European bourses in terms of turnover, Amsterdam is determined not to be among the also-rans expected to go to the wall with the advent of a single-currency super-competitive market.
"The merger will boost Amsterdam's efficiency in both securities and derivatives, increasing liquidity and bolster our international competitive position," De Ranitz said.

"In view of upcoming economic and monetary union, it is of the utmost importance to ensure Amsterdam retains a strong market position. London in particular is a major competitor and we hope that the merger will result in us winning back more trade."

Thanks to an overhaul of its share trading system and the introduction of remote membership for non-Dutch based brokerages, the Amsterdam stock exchange has succeeded in wooing back trade which earlier seeped away to foreign rivals.
Some 70 percent of all turnover in Dutch blue chips is currently conducted via Amsterdam.

De Ranitz said the merger would seek to further reduce trading costs, with major savings being generated through the amalgamation of the bourses' respective clearing, settlement and depositary activities in a single operation.

"We foresee that in the future, clearing, settlement and depositary facilities will become a major factor in the competitive battle," De Ranitz said. "Combining the clearing activities will make them significantly cheaper."

The two exchanges have been flirting with the idea of a merger since the early 1990s but previous attempts to come to an agreement repeatedly foundered over cultural differences as the go-getting options organisation chafed at what it saw as the stock exchange's stuffy attitudes.
"The situation has changed now," EOE's Van Drooge said. "When we last discussed a merger two years ago, the attitude was "do we really have to?". Now it's regarded as a logical next step."
The EOE trades mainly stock and index options but also currency and bond options and index, dollar and bond futures.
Under the planned arrangement, the two exchanges will become operating companies of a new firm, Amsterdam Exchanges (AEX), which will acquire all their outstanding shares.

Existing members will gain a combined 50 percent holding in the new company in the form of cumulative preference shares, with the remaining shares being offered to Dutch listed companies and institutional investors.

The new company will be headed by a four-man executive board comprising a general director and the chairmen of the executive boards of the two bourses and their combined clearing arm. The board will report to an independent supervisory board.
De Ranitz said it was possible the new entity would seek a bourse listing but that there were no immediate plans to do so.
